# Sudhābhojanajātaka (Ja 535)
**ID:** Ja 535
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Sudhābhojanajātaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja535
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sudhābhojanajātaka* (Ja 535) is a birth story set at Jetavana, delivered by the Buddha concerning a liberally minded monk with the opening words “No huckster I” [SuttaCentral]. The narrative centers on the hermit or sage Maccharikosiya ("miserly Kosiya"), who in the tale's lineage is the son and successor of Pañcasikha and the fifth descendant of a wealthy householder reborn as Sakka, alongside other kin reborn as Canda, Suriya, and Mātali [Jones 1952; Luce et al. 1970]. Sent to Kosiya so that he might offer hospitality to whichever is most virtuous, Sakka’s four daughters—personified virtues identified as Āsā (Hope), Saddhā (Faith), Sirī/Lakṣmī (Glory), and Hiri (Shame)—seek his judgment [Luce et al. 1970; Heim 2004]. Kosiya rejects Glory for lavishing unmerited favor on the greedy and foolish, Hope for leading people to disaster, and Faith for being too fickle and easily misplaced, ultimately awarding the gift of food or hospitality to Shame alone [Shaw; Heim 2004]. Anthony Kennedy Warder notes that these personified nymphs in Jātaka No. 535 resemble allegorical characters found in fragments of early Indian Buddhist drama [Warder 2000].
SuttaCentral identifies a full parallel to this narrative in the Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit *Mahāvastu* (Mvu 37, the *Mañjarī Jātaka*), as well as a passage-level parallel in the Pali *Kosiyajātaka* (Ja 470) [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse computations by DharmaNexus confirm extensive shared text between Ja 535 and the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna* (212 matching segments), as well as near-identical verse passages with *Kosiyajātaka* (§1.1–21.4, similarity 0.99) and minor overlaps with the *Vidhurajātaka* (Ja 546) [DharmaNexus]. J. J. Jones also analyzes the character correspondences and lineage differences between the Pali *Sudhābhojanajātaka* and the parallel narrative in the *Mahāvastu* [Jones 1952].
